A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same survey and retain its central taxonomy and conceptual framework. Text, tables, figures, and references support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains a separately labeled appendix.

before.justification: v1 surveys existing research. Numerical findings, including the DigiRL and DistRL improvements, are attributed to cited studies; no original empirical study is reported.

after.justification: Section 6.3 describes calculating averages for Table 11 but also says performance data comes primarily from existing studies. It does not distinguish newly computed analysis results from reproduced scores, leaving the originality of this quantitative synthesis uncertain. No new model experiments are identified.

M1.justification: The contribution remains a survey and taxonomy, without a newly proposed operational agent. Added descriptions of systems such as Mobile-Agent-v3 and ZeroGUI concern cited methods, not changes to an algorithm introduced by this work.

E1.justification: New resources such as JEDI, LearnGUI, and Mobile-Bench-v2 are surveyed rather than used in newly conducted training or testing. Table 11 adds reported scores on benchmarks already discussed in v1, rather than establishing new experimental task coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates a proposed agent against experimental baselines. Table 11 introduces a literature-based comparison of existing systems, but no baseline set for evaluating the paper's own method is added or revised.

E3.justification: Section 6.3 introduces aggregation rules for the new performance comparison: averaging ScreenSpot mobile text/icon scores, macro-averaging GUI-Odyssey results across four splits, and distinguishing AndroidControl single-step success from AndroidWorld task success. These are reporting and aggregation choices, not evidence of experimental reruns.

E4.justification: No new ablations, sensitivity experiments, robustness tests, or empirical case studies are reported. The expanded discussions of benchmark brittleness, interruptions, and evaluation failures are interpretive analyses rather than newly executed tests.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for an original evaluation. Table 11 supplies point scores without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds a substantial numerical comparison in Table 11, absent from v1: examples include UI-R1 at 90.2 on ScreenSpot, UI-TARS-72B at 88.6 on GUI-Odyssey, and Mobile-Agent-v3 at 73.3 on AndroidWorld. These are newly reported literature-derived results, not same-setting improvements over v1. Existing DigiRL and DistRL numerical claims are retained.

T1.justification: The POMDP states, actions, transition probabilities, and observations in v1 Section 3 are retained in v3 Section 4. No new theorem, proof, substantive mathematical definition, or derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, five introductory contributions, and conclusion largely retain their original claims. v3 more explicitly defines the mobile-centered scope and positions its contribution through mobile-specific comparative analysis, including the quantitative benchmark comparison highlighted in Table 1.

C2.justification: New Sections 4.6, 5.3, and 6.4 substantially develop design trade-offs and limitations: perception latency, persistent memory, specialization versus generalization, shallow annotations, unrealistic task scenarios, and unreliable automated judging. Section 7 adds a more detailed security and ethical analysis and connects future directions to the new performance synthesis.

D1.justification: v3 identifies sources and backbone configurations for the new score compilation and expands technical summaries of surveyed systems, including model sizes and training pipelines. These improve documentation without establishing new implementations or changed experimental settings. The existing GitHub collection remains the same resource.

R1.justification: v3 adds a dedicated Related Work section and survey-comparison table, substantially expands coverage of 2025 agents and security research, and explains why selected desktop and web methods inform phone automation. This materially strengthens and revises the survey's positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The narrative gains a standalone related-work section and comparative synthesis subsections following the framework, modeling, and resource reviews. The future-directions section is extensively rewritten around trade-offs and capability gaps, producing substantial structural change despite retention of much earlier descriptive prose.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation, expands the taxonomy and milestone figures, and enlarges existing survey tables. Eight new tables provide comparisons, performance summaries, limitations, and security classifications; Figure 11 adds an automated-evaluation diagram. Many earlier displays remain under new numbering.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's predominantly descriptive treatment by adding structured comparisons of architectural and modeling trade-offs and detailed diagnoses of dataset and evaluation weaknesses. Sections 4.6, 5.3, and 6.4 make the survey more useful for choosing approaches and identifying research gaps. Table 11 also provides a useful numerical overview, although its heterogeneous models and single-step versus whole-task metrics limit the broad claims about RL superiority and online/offline performance. Those limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in analytical depth.
